question: Under TRID, generally how soon after a lender receives a completed loan application must it deliver the Loan Estimate (LE) to the borrower?
choice_a: Within 3 business days of receiving the completed application
choice_b: Within 3 business days before closing
choice_c: Within 30 calendar days of closing, with no earlier deadline
choice_d: There is no federal deadline; timing is left entirely to lender discretion
explanation: Under TRID/Regulation Z, once a lender receives an 'application' (the six pieces of information that trigger the requirement), it generally has 3 business days to deliver the Loan Estimate -- distinct from the separate 3-business-day pre-closing delivery rule that applies to the Closing Disclosure.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated federal TRID/Regulation Z content tested generically on the national portion of the broker exam (national outline Section VII.C.2); not a Pennsylvania-specific statutory rule

question: Which of the following changes after a Closing Disclosure has been issued generally requires a corrected Closing Disclosure AND a new 3-business-day waiting period before consummation?
choice_a: The APR becomes inaccurate beyond the applicable tolerance, the loan product changes, or a prepayment penalty is added
choice_b: Any change of any kind, no matter how minor, to any fee listed on the Closing Disclosure
choice_c: A change to the buyer's chosen moving company
choice_d: A change in the seller's real estate agent
explanation: Under TRID, only three specific changes trigger a new corrected Closing Disclosure and a fresh 3-business-day waiting period before closing: the APR becoming inaccurate beyond tolerance, a change in loan product, and the addition of a prepayment penalty; most other minor corrections can be disclosed at or before closing without restarting the waiting period.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated federal TRID/Regulation Z content tested generically on the national portion of the broker exam (national outline Section VII.C.2); not a Pennsylvania-specific statutory rule

question: Under TRID's fee-tolerance framework, into which category do transfer taxes and fees paid to the lender or a lender affiliate generally fall?
choice_a: Zero tolerance -- these fees generally cannot increase at all between the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure
choice_b: 10% cumulative tolerance -- these fees may increase by up to 10% in the aggregate
choice_c: No tolerance limit whatsoever -- these fees may change by any amount
choice_d: TRID does not regulate these fees at all
explanation: TRID sorts closing costs into three tolerance categories: zero tolerance (fees paid to the creditor/broker or an affiliate, fees for a service the consumer could not shop for, and transfer taxes), a 10% cumulative tolerance (fees for third-party services the consumer could shop for but chose from the lender's provider list, plus recording fees), and fees with no tolerance limit (services the consumer independently shops for and selects a non-listed provider, prepaid interest, and initial escrow deposits).
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated federal TRID/Regulation Z content tested generically on the national portion of the broker exam (national outline Section VII.C.2); not a Pennsylvania-specific statutory rule

question: Does the federal 3-business-day right of rescission under Regulation Z apply to a purchase-money mortgage used to buy a primary residence?
choice_a: No -- the right of rescission generally applies to certain refinances and home-equity transactions on a borrower's principal residence, not to purchase-money mortgages
choice_b: Yes -- every mortgage closing nationwide, including all home purchases, is subject to a 3-business-day rescission period
choice_c: Yes, but only for purchases over $1,000,000
choice_d: No -- the right of rescission was fully repealed nationwide and no longer exists in any transaction
explanation: The Truth in Lending Act's right of rescission generally lets a borrower cancel certain refinance and home-equity-secured transactions on their principal residence within 3 business days of closing; it does not apply to a purchase-money mortgage used to buy the home, since the buyer needs the loan to complete the purchase itself.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated federal TILA/Regulation Z content tested generically on the national portion of the broker exam (national outline Section VII.C); not a Pennsylvania-specific statutory rule

question: Does TRID's integrated Loan Estimate/Closing Disclosure regime apply to an all-cash residential purchase with no financing at all?
choice_a: No -- TRID applies only to most closed-end consumer credit transactions secured by real property; a purely cash transaction with no lender involved is outside its scope
choice_b: Yes -- TRID applies to every residential real estate closing regardless of whether financing is involved
choice_c: Yes, but only if the cash purchase exceeds $500,000
choice_d: TRID applies only to commercial cash transactions, never to residential ones
explanation: TRID's Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure requirements attach to the extension of certain closed-end consumer credit secured by real property; an all-cash purchase with no covered loan involved falls outside TRID's scope, though the parties will still typically use a standard settlement statement for the transaction.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated federal TRID/Regulation Z scope doctrine tested generically on the national portion of the broker exam (national outline Section VII.C.2); not a Pennsylvania-specific statutory rule

question: Under RESPA Section 8, what is a potential consequence for a person who knowingly gives or accepts an illegal kickback for the referral of settlement-service business?
choice_a: Criminal and civil liability, including potential imprisonment of up to one year and fines, in addition to possible civil damages
choice_b: No consequence at all -- RESPA Section 8 sets out a prohibition with no associated penalty
choice_c: Automatic revocation of the buyer's mortgage, regardless of the buyer's own conduct
choice_d: A civil penalty capped at $50, uniformly, regardless of the transaction size
explanation: RESPA Section 8 violations can carry both criminal exposure (fines and/or imprisonment of up to one year) and civil liability (including treble damages in some private actions), reflecting the statute's intent to deter kickbacks and unearned fees tied to referrals of federally related mortgage settlement-service business.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated federal RESPA content tested generically on the national portion of the broker exam (national outline Section VII.C.3); not a Pennsylvania-specific statutory rule

question: Under RESPA Section 9, may a lender require a home-purchase borrower to use a particular title insurance company as a condition of making the loan?
choice_a: No -- RESPA generally prohibits a seller or lender from requiring the buyer, as a condition of sale or loan, to use a particular title insurance company (subject to limited exceptions)
choice_b: Yes, without limitation, whenever the lender prefers a particular title company
choice_c: Yes, but only if the buyer is a first-time homebuyer
choice_d: RESPA does not address title insurance company selection at all
explanation: RESPA Section 9 is a distinct anti-tying provision from Section 8's anti-kickback rule: it generally prohibits conditioning a sale or a federally related mortgage loan on the buyer's use of a specific title insurance company selected by the seller or lender, preserving the consumer's right to shop for title insurance.

choice_b: The owner's policy is always issued completely free of charge

question: What does 'marketable title' generally mean in the context of a real estate closing?
choice_a: Title that is reasonably free from doubt, liens, and encumbrances such that a reasonably prudent buyer would accept it
choice_b: Title that has been advertised for sale in a local newspaper
choice_c: Any title at all, regardless of liens or encumbrances, so long as a deed exists
choice_d: Title held exclusively by a corporation rather than an individual
explanation: Marketable title is title reasonably free from material defects, liens, and encumbrances that would cause a reasonably prudent, informed buyer to decline the property or demand a price reduction -- the standard sale contracts and title commitments require the seller to deliver at closing.

question: What is the primary purpose of a title search (abstract of title) performed before a Pennsylvania closing?
choice_a: To review the recorded chain of title and identify liens, encumbrances, easements, or other defects affecting the property before conveyance
choice_b: To determine the property's current market value for listing purposes
choice_c: To confirm the buyer's credit score with the lender
choice_d: To calculate the buyer's property tax bill for the coming year
explanation: A title search reviews the public record (deeds, mortgages, liens, judgments, easements, and other recorded instruments) affecting a property's chain of title to identify defects or encumbrances that must be resolved -- or disclosed and accepted -- before a marketable title can be conveyed at closing.

question: If a seller has an outstanding money judgment recorded against them in the county where the property is located, what must generally happen before clear, marketable title can be conveyed to the buyer at closing?
choice_a: The judgment lien must generally be satisfied (paid off and released) at or before closing so it no longer encumbers the property
choice_b: Judgment liens automatically expire the moment a sales agreement is signed, with no payoff required
choice_c: The buyer automatically takes title subject to the judgment with no recourse
choice_d: Only the seller's attorney, and no title company, may ever address a judgment lien
explanation: An unresolved judgment lien against the seller attaches to their real property and clouds title; it must generally be satisfied (often paid from sale proceeds at closing) and a release or satisfaction recorded so the buyer receives clear, marketable, insurable title.

question: For priority purposes under Pennsylvania's Mechanics' Lien Law, a properly filed mechanics' lien for construction work generally relates back to what point in time?
choice_a: The date of the first visible construction or commencement of work on the site, not the later date the lien claim itself is filed
choice_b: The date the final invoice is mailed to the property owner
choice_c: The date the property is subsequently resold to a new buyer
choice_d: Mechanics' liens have no priority date at all in Pennsylvania and always rank last
explanation: Under Pennsylvania's Mechanics' Lien Law, a validly perfected mechanics' lien generally relates back in priority to the date visible construction or improvement work began on the property, which can place it ahead of a mortgage or other lien recorded after that commencement date even though the lien claim itself is filed later -- a priority trap closing agents must account for on properties with recent construction.

question: In Pennsylvania residential resale practice, which type of deed is commonly used by institutional or corporate sellers (such as a bank conveying REO property), warranting only against title defects arising during the grantor's own period of ownership?
choice_a: A special warranty deed

choice_c: A sheriff's deed, used in every voluntary residential sale
choice_d: A quitclaim deed, which offers the same protections as a general warranty deed

question: Pennsylvania is generally considered which type of recording-priority state, under which a subsequent bona fide purchaser who takes without notice of a prior unrecorded interest AND records first is generally protected against that earlier, unrecorded interest?
choice_a: A 'race-notice' recording state
choice_b: A 'pure race' recording state, where notice of a prior interest is completely irrelevant
choice_c: A state with no recording statute of any kind
choice_d: A 'pure notice' state where recording order is entirely irrelevant
explanation: Pennsylvania is generally treated as a race-notice recording jurisdiction: to be protected against an earlier unrecorded conveyance, a subsequent purchaser must both take without notice of that earlier interest and record their own instrument first -- a standard recording-priority framework that underlies why prompt recording at closing matters.

question: After a seller's existing mortgage is paid off in full from sale proceeds at closing, what must generally happen to formally clear that mortgage lien from the public record?
choice_a: A satisfaction (or release) of mortgage must generally be recorded with the county Recorder of Deeds

explanation: Paying off a mortgage does not, by itself, remove the lien from the public record; the lender (or its agent) must execute a satisfaction piece (or release), which the closing/settlement agent then records with the county Recorder of Deeds, so the chain of title reflects that the prior mortgage lien no longer encumbers the property.

question: A Pennsylvania closing occurs on April 11 of a non-leap year. The seller has already prepaid the full year's property taxes of $3,650. Using a 365-day proration method where the buyer's ownership period begins on the day of closing (day 101 of the year) through December 31 (265 days), how much should the buyer reimburse the seller at closing for the taxes covering the buyer's period of ownership?
explanation: The daily tax rate is $3,650 / 365 days = $10.00/day. The buyer owns the property for 265 days of the year (day 101 through day 365), so the buyer owes the seller 265 x $10.00 = $2,650 to reimburse the seller for prepaid taxes covering the buyer's period of ownership.
source_note: hedge: standard national real-estate closing-math methodology (365-day proration) applied to an illustrative Pennsylvania closing date; the day-of-closing-belongs-to-buyer convention used here is one of several conventions parties may adopt by contract

question: A Pennsylvania closing occurs on October 1 of a leap year (day 275 of the year). Annual property taxes of $3,660 are due and UNPAID for the year. Using a 366-day proration method where the seller is responsible for taxes accrued through the day before closing (274 days), how much should the seller credit the buyer at closing for the seller's share of the unpaid taxes?

The seller owned the property for 274 days before closing, so the seller owes and must credit the buyer 274 x $10.00 = $2,740 at closing, since the taxes remain unpaid and the buyer will be responsible for paying the full year's bill later.

question: A Pennsylvania seller sells a home for $300,000. The existing mortgage payoff is $180,000, the broker commission is 6% of the sale price ($18,000), and the seller's negotiated share of the realty transfer tax is $1,500. Assuming no other closing costs, what are the seller's approximate net proceeds at closing?
explanation: Net proceeds = sale price minus mortgage payoff minus commission minus the seller's share of transfer tax: $300,000 - $180,000 - $18,000 - $1,500 = $100,500, the amount the seller nets from settlement before accounting for any additional prorations.

question: A buyer purchases a home for $300,000 with a $270,000 loan (90% LTV) and has already paid a $5,000 earnest money deposit, which is credited at closing. The buyer's other closing costs total $6,000. What is the buyer's approximate cash needed to close?
explanation: Down payment = $300,000 - $270,000 = $30,000. Adding closing costs of $6,000 gives $36,000, then subtracting the $5,000 earnest money deposit already paid and credited at closing gives cash to close of $30,000 + $6,000 - $5,000 = $31,000.

question: A rental property being sold has a tenant paying $1,200/month rent, already paid in full for a 30-day month, plus a $1,200 security deposit currently held by the seller. What total amount should the seller credit to the buyer at closing for the unearned rent and the transferred security deposit combined?

The buyer is entitled to rent for the remaining 15 days of the month: 15 x $40.00 = $600 in prorated unearned rent, PLUS the full $1,200 security deposit the seller must transfer to the buyer at closing (since the buyer becomes the new landlord and deposit-holder) = $600 + $1,200 = $1,800 total credit to the buyer.

question: Before closing on a Pennsylvania condominium or planned community unit governed by the Uniform Planned Community Act or Uniform Condominium Act, what disclosure document must the seller generally furnish to the buyer regarding the association's finances and governance?
choice_a: A resale certificate from the unit owners' association, disclosing information such as outstanding assessments, association financial condition, and governing documents
choice_b: Nothing -- Pennsylvania's planned community and condominium statutes impose no seller disclosure obligations of any kind before resale
choice_c: Only a copy of the seller's personal homeowners insurance policy
choice_d: A certificate from the county tax assessor listing only the property's assessed value
explanation: Pennsylvania's Uniform Planned Community Act and Uniform Condominium Act generally require a seller of a unit to furnish the buyer with a resale certificate obtained from the association, disclosing matters such as unpaid assessments, the association's financial condition, pending litigation, and governing documents, so the buyer can evaluate the association before closing.

question: Under generic national closing practice tested on the broker exam, why might a lender require a current survey of the property before closing?
choice_a: To confirm boundary lines, improvements, easements, and encroachments, which can affect both marketability and lender/title insurance requirements
choice_b: Surveys are purely decorative and have no bearing on marketability, financing, or title insurance
choice_c: A survey is required solely to determine the property's paint color scheme
choice_d: Surveys are illegal to obtain in any U.S. state
explanation: A current survey helps confirm the property's boundary lines, the location of improvements relative to those boundaries, and any easements or encroachments -- information lenders and title insurers often want confirmed before closing, since undisclosed boundary or encroachment issues can affect marketability and insurability of title.

question: How does 'table funding' (a term sometimes tested generically alongside wet/dry funding concepts) generally differ from a broker's or correspondent lender's own direct funding of a loan?
choice_a: In table funding, the loan is closed in the originating broker's or correspondent's name but is immediately funded by a separate investor/table funder at or immediately after closing, rather than funded from the originator's own capital
choice_b: Table funding means the loan proceeds are physically handed to the borrower in cash across a literal table at closing
choice_c: Table funding is simply another name for a 30-day dry-funding waiting period
choice_d: Table funding refers exclusively to commercial loans and never applies to residential mortgages
explanation: Table funding describes an arrangement where a loan closes in the name of an originating broker or correspondent lender, but the actual funds come from a separate investor (the 'table funder') at or immediately after closing -- a distinct national mortgage-industry funding-structure concept from the wet-funding/dry-funding classification of how quickly a STATE's closings disburse funds relative to signing.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated national mortgage-industry funding-structure terminology tested generically within the national broker outline's finance subtopics; not a Pennsylvania-specific statutory rule

question: What is a commonly cited best practice, promoted by the CFPB and title/real estate industry groups, for protecting buyers and sellers against wire fraud targeting closing funds?
choice_a: Independently verify wire transfer instructions by phone, using a previously known and trusted phone number, before sending any closing funds -- never relying solely on emailed instructions
choice_b: Always send closing funds immediately upon receiving any emailed wire instructions, without any independent verification
choice_c: Wire fraud at real estate closings is a myth with no documented cases, so no precautions are necessary
choice_d: Only cash payments should ever be used at closing; wire transfers are prohibited nationwide
explanation: Because closing-related business email compromise/wire fraud has become a well-documented risk, the CFPB and real estate/title industry groups commonly recommend independently verifying wire instructions by phone (using a previously known, trusted number -- not a number provided in the same email as the instructions) before sending or accepting any closing funds by wire.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated CFPB consumer-guidance and national real-estate/title-industry wire-fraud-prevention best practices; not a specific statutory mandate

question: Before a deed can generally be accepted for recording with a Pennsylvania county Recorder of Deeds, what must the deed typically include beyond the grantor's signature?
choice_a: A proper acknowledgment (notarization) of the grantor's signature
choice_b: Nothing further -- an unnotarized, unacknowledged signature is always sufficient for recording anywhere in Pennsylvania
choice_c: The buyer's fingerprint in ink, in lieu of any notarization
choice_d: A separate court order authorizing the recording in every transaction
explanation: Consistent with recording practice nationwide, a Pennsylvania deed generally must be properly acknowledged (notarized) before a county Recorder of Deeds will accept it for recording, since the acknowledgment helps establish the document's authenticity for the public record.
